items.title: AI Fact-Checks Elon's Flying Roadster
items.vendor_flag: The show states the hosts are AI-generated characters. All Tesla figures are the show's reading of Tesla's livestream, not independently verified here.
items.reader_fit: Low. A UK recruiter gets only a transferable method for stress-testing a vendor demo and reading pre-payment terms, nothing recruiting-specific.

points.claim: Check whether a vendor's own numbers agree with each other before believing a demo.
points.evidence: Screen said 4,700 kg of suction; Tesla's stated pull of up to 2G would imply a 2,350 kg car; an engineer said just under 1,700 kg
points.quote: Tesla says the fans pull up to 2G. The screen said 4700. If that's 2G, the car weighs 2350. Their engineer said under 1700.

points.claim: Headline performance was not independently timed, and the recorded run differed from the claim.
points.evidence: Tesla showed 0.81 seconds; a recorded run said one second flat
points.quote: Nobody outside Tesla timed it.

points.claim: Pre-order terms: money down for a product with no price and no guaranteed date.
points.evidence: $5,000 on a card, $45,000 by wire within ten days, or a quarter million up front; first $5,000 fully refundable; contract says delivery date cannot be guaranteed
points.quote: Five grand on a card, 45 more by wire in ten days, or a quarter million up front for the thruster trim.

points.claim: The show's proposed buyer protections: escrow, interest on lateness, neutral on-camera test, then sell.
points.evidence: Escrow deposits; pay interest every year late; neutral tester on camera; thrusters off public roads until a regulator signs off
points.quote: Show, then sell.

items.title: AI Just Broke The Internet. For Real This Time.
items.guest_line: none (hosts Kevin Pereira and Gavin Purcell)
items.vendor_flag: Gavin Purcell says Fal is not a sponsor but gave him credits, so his praise of the Fal-hosted video models is not fully neutral. Exploit-attempt figures are relayed second-hand from Cloudflare's CEO. Product names are ASR-garbled in places.
items.reader_fit: Low to moderate. Useful context on agent access risk and AI video cost, but nothing recruiting-specific; a UK recruiter would use it only as general AI-awareness background.

points.claim: Once a vulnerability is public, exploit attempts scale from thousands to over a million within hours because agents pile on.
points.evidence: Cloudflare's Matthew Prince as relayed by a host: thousands of attempts, tens of thousands within 45 minutes of the announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, supposedly over a million
points.quote: That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement. And then hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and supposedly now well over a million.

points.claim: Banks reportedly see people's personal AI agents acting in accounts as unauthorised.
points.evidence: Axios report, sourced to a bunch of banks, as described by Gavin Purcell; the hosts say banks are unsure the use cases are approved by users
points.quote: AI agents are unauthorized using bank software and this was from a bunch of banks

points.claim: A Chinese-origin video model, Wan 3, was claimed to cost about a fifth of Seedance 2.5 on Fal, with somewhat less realistic output.
points.evidence: About a fifth of the price; Seedance 2.5 judged more realistic in a single identically-prompted text-to-video test
points.quote: the Waon video is not bad and there's a little level of like it's getting something interesting and for a fifth the price, that is a big deal, right?

points.claim: Claude Duet is pitched as a separate, proactive work agent; the hosts are cautious about trust and token spend.
points.evidence: Dedicated app, waitlist, not rolled out to everybody; proactivity is the pitched differentiator
points.quote: I think the differentiator as they're pitching it is the proactivity of it.

items.title: AI Is Moving Too Fast. Two New Models In Two Weeks?!
items.guest_line: none (hosts Kevin Pereira and Gavin Purcell)
items.vendor_flag: No guest. Model names are fictional-seeming future products as spoken in the transcript and ASR spellings vary (Carbon, Argon, Terra, Kadamari). Kevin Pereira built the demo himself with the model he is reviewing.
items.reader_fit: Low. General AI-model landscape for a UK recruiter; the only practical angle is how to use cheaper model tiers and why to treat benchmark claims for gated models with caution.

points.claim: OpenAI's GPT-6.1 line is tiered like Anthropic's, with Terra as the mid-tier.
points.evidence: Astra top, Saul second (Opus-level), Terra (Sonnet-level), Luna lowest (Haiku-level)
points.quote: Terra is kind of their sonnet level and then there's Luna which is very much like the haiku lowest level.

points.claim: The mid-tier model was fast at computer use but struggled to follow a creative brief, so a bigger model had to rewrite the brief.
points.evidence: Kevin Pereira's Katamari-style demo built via Blender; Terra described as very fast for computer use
points.quote: just go ask it how to fix it and Astra came back and was like oh you should build it in this way

points.claim: Cheap intelligence lets you generate many variants and then select and merge, instead of perfecting one.
points.evidence: Example: 50 fonts and 50 interactive treatments, pick 10, merge into one; or a hundred versions of a graphic and pick version 73
points.quote: here are 50 fonts and 50 different like interactive ways that these graphics could play out. I picked these 10 as my favorite. Now merge those into one.

points.claim: Benchmark claims for a model most people cannot use are weak evidence.
points.evidence: Gemini 4 Carbon was only available to a cyber-defence group at the time; Gavin Purcell argues for waiting until a model is widely available before judging it
points.quote: you should wait to talk about your models until they are in the hands of everybody

items.title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF
items.guest_line: Rob Snyder · Author of The Power of Pull, writer of The Physics of Startups
items.vendor_flag: Rob Snyder is promoting his own book and newsletter and the 50-startups claim is his own. The episode carries WorkOS and DX sponsor reads, which are not editorial. No third-party product is praised by its vendor.
items.reader_fit: Moderate. A UK recruiter selling a service or building an internal TA product gets a practical discovery-call structure and LinkedIn outreach benchmarks, plus an applicant tracking system example; the rest is founder-focused.

points.claim: Real pull needs all four of Project, Unavoidable, List of options and Limitations at once.
points.evidence: Jump (AI notetaker for financial advisers): advisers must put notes in a CRM or could go to jail; generic notetakers were not CRM-integrated or clearly SEC-compliant. Insurance agents lacked the Unavoidable element
points.quote: You need all four at once.

points.claim: Cold LinkedIn outreach targets: about 100 to 150 connection requests a week, with acceptance and reply rates to check against.
points.evidence: Rob's typical targets: 30 to 40% accept; of those 30 to 50% reply; he aims for two to three customer conversations a day
points.quote: like 30 to 40% of them should accept your connection request and then of them 30 to 50 should% should reply

points.claim: AI personalisation in first-touch outreach has not worked for him at this stage.
points.evidence: Says it tells people something they already know and reads like Claude wrote it; the message only needs to be interesting enough to get a call
points.quote: I uh have not seen AI personalization work at this stage.

points.claim: When a prospect is lukewarm, ask the Hail Mary question: is there anything on your to-do list you would pay me to do right now?
points.evidence: An applicant tracking system startup selling to governments: the buyer answered with a job description task that became their first contract
points.quote: yeah, what I'd actually pay you to solve is this like job description thing right now. And that became their first contract.

points.claim: Avoid design partners: they give feedback but do not buy.
points.evidence: Rob says he has yet to see design partners help; real buyers want the job done, not to help build
points.quote: they give a bunch of feedback and never buy from you

items.title: A UGC masterclass from the 22-year-old who built Wispr Flow's growth machine
items.guest_line: Hector Serrano · Head of Content @ Wispr Flow
items.vendor_flag: Hector Serrano works for Wispr Flow and praises its growth programme and the Tribe tool he uses; revenue growth of 30x and the $2 billion valuation come from the host and episode description, not verified. Creator earnings of $13,000 a month are his own claim. Episode carries WorkOS and DX sponsor reads.
items.reader_fit: Moderate to high. Hiring signals for social-first roles, manual DM sourcing numbers, and a retainer-plus-commission structure transfer directly to UK agency or in-house recruiters sourcing creators or building an employer brand.

points.claim: Pair a quota-based retainer with uncapped commission so new creators stay long enough to break out.
points.evidence: Example: 25 videos for $1,500 if the quota is hit; top-ups depend on commission earned; best creators earn about $13,000 a month (his claim)
points.quote: we're going to pay you $1,500 as long as you hit that quota of videos

points.claim: Source creators by targeted, manual DMs off-platform: roughly 150 to 250 a week for five or six good ones.
points.evidence: 150 to 250 DMs over a week yielded five or six good creators; he prefers manual outreach to mass software; also asks good creators for referrals via their follows
points.quote: from those 150 to 250 DMs, you're probably going to get like five or six really good creators.

points.claim: For a social-first hire, the screen is simple: has the candidate grown an account to around 10,000 followers, and are they hard-working and a good fit.
points.evidence: Minimum follower floor of 10,000 to 15,000; Instagram a stronger signal than TikTok; he and a colleague had very different CVs (2.5 GPA vs 4.0)
points.quote: has this person grown an account, even if it's like 10,000 followers?

points.claim: Posting a salary and requirements that are too high attracts the wrong people for this kind of role.
points.evidence: Example of 250k or 200k base with generous equity as the mistake; he and a colleague joined as interns
points.quote: you're going to end up attracting the wrong type of people

points.claim: He hires through his own social channels: his videographer and creators came from Instagram stories.
points.evidence: Videographer found via an Instagram story posted in May, flown to San Francisco on three days' notice
points.quote: I hired them from my Instagram stories.

gaps: AI For Humans transcripts are ASR with unnamed speakers; product names (Waon/Wan, SeaDance/Seedance, Kaedim/Fal, Kadamari/Katamari) are garbled and were normalised only in claims, never in quotes.
Episode 2026-10-20 is a scripted debate by AI-generated characters; Tesla figures are the show's own and not independently verified.

Revenue growth of 30x and the $2bn valuation for Wispr Flow come from the host and description, not evidence in the transcript beyond the host's remark; creator earnings of $13,000 a month are Serrano's own claim.
